amc8-2004-01.title: Find the scale
amc8-2004-01.body:
$72 \div 12 = 6$, so each centimeter stands for $6$ km. Then $17$ cm stands for $17 \times 6 = 102$ km.

**Answer: (B) 102**

amc8-2004-02.title: Choose the first digit
amc8-2004-02.body:
The first digit cannot be $0$, so it is $2$ or $4$. If it is $2$, the remaining digits $0, 0, 4$ can be arranged in $3$ ways ($004, 040, 400$). Likewise $3$ ways if it is $4$. Total $3 + 3 = 6$.

**Answer: (B) 6**

amc8-2004-03.title: Food per meal
amc8-2004-03.body:
$12$ meals feed $18$ people, so each meal feeds $\frac{18}{12} = 1.5$ people. To feed $12$ people they need $12 \div 1.5 = 8$ meals.

**Answer: (A) 8**

amc8-2004-03.title: Scale down
amc8-2004-03.body:
$12$ meals for $18$ people is the same as $2$ meals for $3$ people. For $12 = 4 \times 3$ people they need $4 \times 2 = 8$ meals.

**Answer: (A) 8**

amc8-2004-04.title: Choose who sits out
amc8-2004-04.body:
Picking the $3$ starters is the same as picking the $1$ player who does not start. There are $4$ choices for that player, so $4$ ways.

**Answer: (B) 4**

amc8-2004-05.title: One loser per game
amc8-2004-05.body:
Every game eliminates exactly one team, and in the end $15$ of the $16$ teams have been eliminated. So $15$ games are played.

**Answer: (D) 15**

amc8-2004-06.title: Count made shots
amc8-2004-06.body:
After $20$ shots she made $0.55 \times 20 = 11$. After $25$ shots she made $0.56 \times 25 = 14$. So she made $14 - 11 = 3$ of the last $5$.

**Answer: (C) 3**

amc8-2004-07.title: Compute
amc8-2004-07.body:
Maximum heart rate: $220 - 26 = 194$. Target: $0.8 \times 194 = 155.2$, which rounds to $155$.

**Answer: (B) 155**

amc8-2004-07.title: Estimate
amc8-2004-07.body:
$80\%$ of about $200$ is $160$, and $80\%$ of $194$ is a bit less: $160 - 0.8 \times 6 = 155.2 \approx 155$.

**Answer: (B) 155**

amc8-2004-08.title: List them
amc8-2004-08.body:
The tens digit can be $1$ to $7$ and then the units digit is fixed: $16, 25, 34, 43, 52, 61, 70$. That is $7$ numbers.

**Answer: (B) 7**

amc8-2004-09.title: Use totals
amc8-2004-09.body:
The five numbers add to $5 \times 54 = 270$. The first two add to $2 \times 48 = 96$. The last three add to $270 - 96 = 174$, so their average is $174 \div 3 = 58$.

**Answer: (D) 58**

amc8-2004-09.title: Balance the deviations
amc8-2004-09.body:
The first two are each $6$ below $54$ on average, a total of $12$ below. The last three must make up $12$ above, i.e. $4$ each: $54 + 4 = 58$.

**Answer: (D) 58**

amc8-2004-10.title: Add the minutes
amc8-2004-10.body:
Monday $75$ min, Tuesday $50$ min, Wednesday $8{:}20$ to $10{:}45$ is $145$ min, Friday $30$ min. Total $75 + 50 + 145 + 30 = 300$ minutes $= 5$ hours. Pay: $5 \times 3 = 15$ dollars.

**Answer: (E) \$15**

amc8-2004-11.title: Who can be at the ends?
amc8-2004-11.body:
The ends cannot be $12$ (largest: it is in place 2 or 3), cannot be $-2$ (smallest: it is in place 3 or 4), and cannot be $6$ (the median). So the first and last numbers are $4$ and $9$ in some order, and their average is $\frac{4 + 9}{2} = 6.5$.

(One valid order: $4, 12, -2, 6, 9$.)

**Answer: (C) 6.5**

amc8-2004-12.title: Fractions of the battery
amc8-2004-12.body:
Idle, the phone uses $\frac{1}{24}$ of the battery per hour; talking it uses $\frac13$ per hour. In the $9$ hours she was idle $8$ hours and talked $1$ hour, using $\frac{8}{24} + \frac13 = \frac13 + \frac13 = \frac23$. The remaining $\frac13$ of the battery lasts $\frac13 \times 24 = 8$ more idle hours.

**Answer: (B) 8**

amc8-2004-12.title: Units of charge
amc8-2004-12.body:
Say a full battery is $24$ units: idle uses $1$ unit/hour, talking uses $8$ units/hour. She used $8 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 8 = 16$ units, leaving $8$ units, which last $8$ idle hours.

**Answer: (B) 8**

amc8-2004-13.title: Test each statement
amc8-2004-13.body:
- If I is true, Bill is the oldest, so Amy is not the oldest and II is also true — two true statements. So I is false.
- If II is the true one, then Amy is not oldest and (I false) Bill is not oldest, so Celine is the oldest — but then III is true too. So II is false.
- So III is the true one: Amy **is** the oldest (II false), and Celine is not the youngest, so Celine is second and Bill is youngest.

Order: Amy, Celine, Bill (check: I false, II false, III true).

**Answer: (E) Amy, Celine, Bill**

amc8-2004-13.title: Check the choices
amc8-2004-13.body:
Count true statements for each choice: (A) Bill, Amy, Celine: I, II true. (B) Amy, Bill, Celine: none true. (C) Celine, Amy, Bill: II, III true. (D) Celine, Bill, Amy: II, III true. (E) Amy, Celine, Bill: only III true. Only (E) works.

**Answer: (E) Amy, Celine, Bill**

amc8-2004-14.title: Box and subtract

amc8-2004-15.title: Count the new ring
amc8-2004-15.body:
The figure has a center tile and two rings of $6$ and $12$ tiles. Each ring of hexagons has $6$ more tiles than the one inside it, so the new border has $18$ white tiles. White: $6 + 18 = 24$; black: $13$. Difference: $24 - 13 = 11$.

**Answer: (C) 11**

amc8-2004-15.title: Count along the sides
amc8-2004-15.body:
The new border is a hexagon with $4$ tiles on each side. Going around, each of the $6$ sides contributes $3$ new tiles (not counting the shared corner twice): $6 \times 3 = 18$ tiles. Then $(6 + 18) - 13 = 11$.

**Answer: (C) 11**

amc8-2004-16.title: Use milliliters
amc8-2004-16.body:
Juice: $\frac13 \cdot 600 = 200$ mL and $\frac25 \cdot 600 = 240$ mL, total $440$ mL. The mixture is $1200$ mL. Fraction: $\frac{440}{1200} = \frac{11}{30}$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{11}{30}$**

amc8-2004-16.title: Average the fractions
amc8-2004-16.body:
Both pitchers have the same volume, so the fraction of juice is the average: $\frac12\left(\frac13 + \frac25\right) = \frac12 \cdot \frac{11}{15} = \frac{11}{30}$.

**Answer: (C) $\frac{11}{30}$**

amc8-2004-17.title: List by the first friend
Stars and bars
amc8-2004-17.body:
Give each friend one pencil first; then share the remaining $3$ pencils freely among $3$ friends: $\binom{3+2}{2} = 10$ ways.

**Answer: (D) 10**

amc8-2004-18.title: Start with the smallest scores
amc8-2004-18.body:
The ten throws use each of $1$–$10$ exactly once.
- Ben $4 = 1 + 3$ (the only way with different numbers).
- Cindy $7$: $1+6$, $3+4$ use Ben's numbers, so $7 = 2 + 5$.
- Dave $11$: $1+10$, $2+9$, $3+8$, $5+6$ all reuse a number, so $11 = 4 + 7$.
- Ellen $17 = 8 + 9$ (since $7 + 10$ uses Dave's $7$).
- Alice gets the rest: $6 + 10 = 16$. ✓

Alice hits the $6$.

**Answer: (A) Alice**

amc8-2004-18.title: Who could have the 6?
amc8-2004-18.body:
Partner of $6$ would be: Ben $-2$ (no), Cindy $1$, Dave $5$, Ellen $11$ (no), Alice $10$. Ben must be $1+3$, so Cindy can't use $1$; Cindy must then be $2+5$, so Dave can't use $5$. Only Alice is left.

**Answer: (A) Alice**

amc8-2004-19.title: Use the LCM
amc8-2004-19.body:
The number minus $2$ is divisible by $3, 4, 5, 6$, i.e. by $\text{lcm}(3,4,5,6) = 60$. The smallest such number larger than $2$ is $60 + 2 = 62$, which lies between $60$ and $79$.

**Answer: (B) 60 and 79**

amc8-2004-20.title: Work from the chairs
amc8-2004-20.body:
The $6$ empty chairs are the remaining $\frac14$ of the chairs, so there are $24$ chairs and $18$ are occupied. These $18$ seated people are $\frac23$ of everyone, so there are $18 \div \frac23 = 27$ people.

**Answer: (D) 27**

amc8-2004-20.title: Algebra
amc8-2004-20.body:
Let $p$ people, $c$ chairs. $\frac23 p = \frac34 c$ and $\frac14 c = 6$. So $c = 24$, $\frac23 p = 18$, $p = 27$.

**Answer: (D) 27**

amc8-2004-21.title: Complement
amc8-2004-21.body:
The product is odd only if both numbers are odd: $P = \frac24 \cdot \frac23 = \frac13$. So $P(\text{even}) = 1 - \frac13 = \frac23$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac23$**

amc8-2004-21.title: Count outcomes
amc8-2004-21.body:
There are $4 \times 3 = 12$ equally likely pairs. Odd products need $A \in \{1,3\}$ and $B \in \{1,3\}$: $4$ pairs. Even: $12 - 4 = 8$, so $\frac{8}{12} = \frac23$.

**Answer: (D) $\frac23$**

amc8-2004-22.title: Pick a convenient number
amc8-2004-22.body:
Suppose there are $5$ women: $2$ single and $3$ married. Each married woman is there with her husband, so there are $3$ men. Total $5 + 3 = 8$ people, and $\frac38$ are married men.

**Answer: (B) $\frac38$**

amc8-2004-23.title: Follow her run
amc8-2004-23.body:
Counterclockwise from $J$ she goes $J \to K \to L \to M \to J$.
- Along $JK$ her distance grows steadily.
- Along $KL$ it keeps growing, up to the diagonal $JL$ at corner $L$ (the farthest point).
- Along $LM$ it shrinks to $JM$.
- Along $MJ$ it shrinks to $0$.

So the graph rises from $0$ to a single peak and returns to $0$. (A) never comes back, (B) does not start at $0$, (C) has two peaks, (E) never comes back. Only (D) fits.

**Answer: (D)**

amc8-2004-24.title: Area two ways
amc8-2004-24.body:
Area of $EFGH$ = rectangle minus four corner triangles: $80 - 2\cdot\frac12\cdot4\cdot3 - 2\cdot\frac12\cdot6\cdot5 = 80 - 12 - 30 = 38$.

The base $HE$ is the hypotenuse of a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle, so $HE = 5$. With $d$ as the height to base $HE$: $5d = 38$, $d = 7.6$.

**Answer: (C) 7.6**

amc8-2004-25.title: Union minus circle
amc8-2004-25.body:
Each square has area $16$. They overlap in a $2 \times 2$ square (each side is bisected), so together they cover $16 + 16 - 4 = 28$.

The two intersection points are opposite corners of this $2 \times 2$ square, so the circle's diameter is its diagonal $2\sqrt2$ and the radius is $\sqrt2$. Circle area $= \pi(\sqrt2)^2 = 2\pi$.

Shaded area $= 28 - 2\pi$.

**Answer: (D) $28-2\pi$**
